title: Jeremiah 45:1–5
context: Jeremiah gives a brief message from the LORD to Baruch, his scribe. It is dated to the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when Baruch wrote Jeremiah's words in a book, which links it with the scroll account of chapter 36, even though it is placed here after the events in Egypt of chapters 43–44. Baruch had lamented that the LORD added sorrow to his pain. The LORD answers that he is tearing down what he built in the whole land, tells Baruch not to seek great things for himself, and promises him his life wherever he goes. The word is pastoral counsel for a faithful servant in a time of collapse.

verses.text: The message that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah, when he wrote these words in a book at the mouth of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: "The message that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah." Arminian readers note that the setting is the writing of Jeremiah's words "in a book," which chapter 36 describes in the same fourth year of Jehoiakim.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this short chapter stands out of chronological order, placed after the later events in Egypt. They suggest it may close a section of the book, but hold that suggestion loosely since the text does not explain the placement.

verses.text: “The LORD, the God of Israel, says to you, Baruch:
verses.arminianNotes: "The LORD, the God of Israel, says to you, Baruch." Arminian readers see the LORD addressing a single servant by name in the middle of national catastrophe, showing personal care for those who serve him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the God of Israel, who rules nations, speaks a personal word to a scribe. God's sovereign purposes include tender attention to individual servants.

verses.text: ‘You said, “Woe is me now! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain! I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: "Woe is me now!" Arminian readers see Baruch's honest complaint that the LORD "has added sorrow to my pain." Faithful service has brought him weariness rather than relief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD quotes Baruch's own lament back to him. Baruch's complaint is not ignored or condemned; it is heard and answered, as Jeremiah's own complaints were.

verses.text: “You shall tell him, the LORD says: ‘Behold, that which I have built, I will break down, and that which I have planted I will pluck up; and this in the whole land.
verses.arminianNotes: "Behold, that which I have built, I will break down." Arminian readers see the LORD explaining that Baruch's pain is part of a larger grief: God himself is tearing down what he planted "in the whole land."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the echo of Jeremiah's call in 1:10, "to uproot and to tear down." The LORD's sorrow over the land puts Baruch's personal sorrow in perspective.

verses.text: Do you seek great things for yourself? Don’t seek them; for, behold, I will bring evil on all flesh,’ says the LORD, ‘but I will let you escape with your life wherever you go.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: "Do you seek great things for yourself? Don’t seek them." Arminian readers see pastoral counsel: in a time of collapse, Baruch should not cling to personal ambition, but receive the gift of his life with gratitude.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same counsel and note the promise, "I will let you escape with your life wherever you go," similar to the word to Ebed-melech in 39:18. Both traditions treat this as shared ground, not a debate over ambition.
